newsitem.title: INDIA: India's prime minister meets Pakistani diplomat.
newsitem.headline: India's prime minister meets Pakistani diplomat.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda met Pakistan's top diplomat on Saturday in an apparent sign that talks between foreign ministry officials of the rival neighbours have begun well.
Deve Gowda spent about half an hour with Pakistani foreign secretary Shamshad Ahmad at his residence in New Delhi. The two men sat on separate sofas as they posed for photographers.
Talks between Ahmad and his Indian opposite number Salman Haidar were expected to resume for a second day later on Saturday, an official said.
Deve Gowda told visiting South African President Nelson Mandela on Friday of New Delhi's desire to normalise ties with Islamabad to their "mutual advantage".

The talks are the first since January 1994, when a dialogue foundered on Kashmir. Tension over the disputed Himalayan region sparked two of the three wars the two countries, now threshold nuclear powers, have fought since independence in 1947.
Both sides remained tight-lipped after Friday's two-hour session, but emphasised that the atmosphere had been cordial.
Haidar told reporters all issues had been discussed, repeating the same formula when asked if they included Kashmir.
The Press Trust of India (PTI) news agency quoted "informed sources" as saying the Pakistanis had reiterated their demand for a referendum in the Indian state of Jammu and Kashmir.
PTI said the Indians ruled out any compromise on the state's territorial integrity with India and "told Islamabad to stop the proxy war through sponsored terrorism in Jammu and Kashmir".
India accuses Pakistan of arming, training and financing Kashmiri Moslem separatist guerrillas fighting a seven-year-old insurgency in the two-thirds of Kashmir controlled by India.
Pakistan, which holds the rest of Kashmir, denies the charge, but has pledged to continue what it calls moral, political and diplomatic support for the Kashmiris.
Pakistan's chief of army staff General Jehangir Karamat said this week Pakistani troops would not pull back from the disputed Siachen Glacier, where they are confronting Indian forces.
Karamat linked any withdrawal from Siachen, the world's highest battlefield, to a settlement of the Kashmir issue.
India wants to put Kashmir on the back-burner and focus on trade and economic cooperation. Pakistan sees "progress" on Kashmir as an essential part of any deal.

"Except for the hardliners, and there are enough of those in both countries, there is a growing consensus that the neighbours should work on the areas where there is scope for improvement," said an editorial in The Asian Age newspaper.

Kashmiri separatists in the umbrella Hurriyat organisation staged a strike in Srinagar for a second day on Saturday to protest at their exclusion from the talks. Witnesses said shops closed in the city, the summer capital of Jammu and Kashmir.
Shabir Ahmad Shah, a separatist leader detained on Friday during a march by 100 Hurriyat supporters, was later released.
Police also detained, and later freed, a dozen Hurriyat leaders, including the group's chairman Mirwaiz Omar Farooq, in New Delhi to block a planned protest near the talks venue.
Farooq said the All Parties Hurriyat (freedom) Conference did not oppose rapprochement between India and Pakistan, but wanted Kashmiris to be part of any talks on their homeland.
"We don't see this as a bilateral issue," he told Reuters by telephone. "It's not a territorial or regional dispute they can discuss by themselves...The Kashmiris must be involved."
